TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) are both core protocols used for sending data over the internet, but they handle data transmission very differently. 

TCP is a connection-oriented protocol. Before sending data, it establishes a reliable connection through a "three-way handshake." It guarantees that packets arrive in the correct order and resends any lost data, making it ideal for applications like web browsing, emails, and file transfers where accuracy is critical. However, this reliability introduces latency.

UDP, in contrast, is a connectionless protocol. It simply blasts data to the receiver without checking if it arrived or if it is in the correct order. While this makes it faster, it lacks reliability. UDP is best suited for real-time applications—such as video streaming, online gaming, and VoIP—where speed matters more than dropping an occasional packet.
